title: Crypto & Blockchain Foundations
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: A blockchain is a distributed, append-only ledger maintained by many computers (nodes) with no central authority — records are grouped into blocks, cryptographically chained so altering history is computationally infeasible. Cryptocurrency is a digital asset native to a blockchain. Key properties: decentralization (no single controller), immutability (history can't be changed), transparency (public ledger), and trustlessness (rules enforced by code, not institutions). Bitcoin (2009) introduced digital scarcity — solving the 'double-spend' problem without a bank. Public/private keys control ownership: your private key IS your money — lose it, lose everything.

WORKED EXAMPLE: To send Bitcoin, you sign a transaction with your private key. The network verifies the signature and that you haven't already spent those coins, then records it permanently. No bank approves it — thousands of nodes independently agree it's valid. This 'consensus without trust' is the core innovation, replacing an institution with math and incentives.

PRACTICE: 1) Explain how a blockchain makes altering history infeasible. 2) Describe why 'your keys, your coins' matters. 3) Explain the double-spend problem Bitcoin solved.

title: How Blockchains Work: Consensus & Mining
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Consensus mechanisms let a decentralized network agree on truth. Proof of Work (Bitcoin): miners compete to solve a hard math puzzle; the winner adds the next block and earns rewards — secure but energy-intensive. Proof of Stake (Ethereum post-2022): validators stake capital as collateral; misbehavior is punished by 'slashing' — far more energy-efficient. Hash functions link blocks and secure data. The 51% attack: controlling most mining/staking power could rewrite history — economically prohibitive on large chains. Block time and finality determine how fast transactions confirm.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A miner spends real electricity to find a valid block hash. If they tried to cheat with a fraudulent block, other nodes reject it and their electricity is wasted for nothing. The system aligns incentives: honest mining is profitable, cheating is costly. Security comes from making attacks more expensive than the reward — economics, not permission.

PRACTICE: 1) Compare Proof of Work vs Proof of Stake. 2) Explain why a 51% attack is economically deterred. 3) Describe how hashing links blocks.

title: Wallets, Security & Self-Custody
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: A wallet stores your private keys, not the coins (coins live on-chain). Hot wallets (connected, convenient, riskier) vs cold wallets (offline, secure, for savings). Seed phrase (12-24 words) can regenerate your entire wallet — guard it like the master key it is; anyone with it owns your funds. 'Not your keys, not your coins': funds on an exchange are controlled by the exchange, which can freeze, lose, or be hacked. Common threats: phishing, fake apps, SIM swaps, and social engineering. Security is personal responsibility — there's no fraud department to reverse a mistaken or stolen transaction.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A user keeps life savings on an exchange for convenience. The exchange collapses (as several have), and the funds are gone — legally the user was an unsecured creditor, not an owner. Someone using a hardware wallet with a securely stored seed phrase kept full control throughout. The difference between custody models is the difference between owning and merely trusting.

PRACTICE: 1) Explain the difference between hot and cold wallets. 2) Describe why a seed phrase must never be shared or stored online. 3) Explain 'not your keys, not your coins.'

title: Ethereum, Smart Contracts & DeFi
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Ethereum extended blockchain from money to programmable contracts — smart contracts are self-executing code that runs exactly as written, enabling apps without intermediaries. 'Gas' fees pay for computation. Decentralized Finance (DeFi) rebuilds financial services (lending, trading, borrowing) as open protocols: DEXs (decentralized exchanges), lending platforms, stablecoins (crypto pegged to $1), and yield farming. Composability ('money legos') lets protocols stack. Risks are real: smart-contract bugs, exploits, impermanent loss, and unsustainable yields. Code is law — a bug can drain funds with no recourse.

WORKED EXAMPLE: On a DeFi lending protocol, you deposit crypto and earn interest, or borrow against collateral — all executed by code, no bank, available 24/7 globally. But if the smart contract has a vulnerability, an attacker can drain it in seconds, and there's no fraud reversal. DeFi offers permissionless access at the cost of removing the safety nets institutions provide.

title: Tokens, NFTs & Digital Assets
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Tokens represent assets or utility on a blockchain. Fungible tokens (interchangeable, like currency — ERC-20 standard) vs non-fungible tokens (NFTs — unique, ERC-721, representing ownership of a specific digital or real item). Tokenomics: supply schedule, distribution, utility, and incentives determine a token's economic soundness — most tokens fail on weak tokenomics. Utility tokens (access/function) vs security tokens (investment, regulated) vs governance tokens (voting rights). NFTs enable provable digital ownership, but value depends on demand, not the technology itself. Beware: most tokens and NFTs go to zero.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A project launches a token with no real utility and 90% held by insiders. Early hype pumps the price; insiders sell into the demand; the price collapses. Sound tokenomics — genuine utility, fair distribution, aligned incentives — is what separates a durable token from a pump-and-dump. The technology is neutral; the economic design determines survival.

title: Trading, Markets & Risk
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Crypto markets trade 24/7, are highly volatile, and are driven by sentiment, liquidity, and narratives as much as fundamentals. Market cycles: accumulation, run-up, euphoria/bubble, crash, capitulation — extreme greed and fear repeat. Risk management is survival: position sizing, never investing more than you can afford to lose, and avoiding leverage (which liquidates you on normal volatility). Common losses: FOMO buying tops, panic selling bottoms, leverage liquidation, scams, and rug pulls. Volatility means 50-80% drawdowns are normal even in assets that later recover — most people sell at the worst time.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A trader uses 10x leverage. A normal 10% price move against them wipes out 100% of their position — liquidated — even though the asset recovers days later. Unleveraged, they'd have simply ridden it out. Leverage turns survivable volatility into permanent loss, which is why it destroys most crypto traders regardless of whether their long-term thesis was right.

title: Grandmaster — Regulation, Scams & Due Diligence
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: The regulatory landscape is evolving and varies by country — securities laws, taxes (crypto is taxable; every trade can be a taxable event), and AML/KYC rules apply. Due diligence separates real projects from scams: examine the team (doxxed vs anonymous), the actual product/traction, tokenomics, audits, and community. Red flags: guaranteed returns, pressure to buy now, anonymous teams with big promises, unaudited contracts, and unsustainable yields. Common scams: rug pulls (developers drain funds), Ponzi schemes (paying old investors with new money), phishing, and fake giveaways. 'If it sounds too good to be true, it is' applies with full force.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A project promises 'guaranteed 2% daily returns.' The math is impossible (that's 137,000% annually) — it can only pay early investors with later investors' money until it collapses (a Ponzi). Recognizing that no legitimate investment guarantees such returns is the single most protective piece of due diligence. Impossible math is the clearest scam signal.

title: King Level — Blockchain's Future & Strategic Understanding
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: At the highest level, understanding crypto means separating durable innovation from speculation and hype. Genuine use cases: borderless payments, censorship-resistant money, programmable finance, verifiable digital ownership, supply-chain transparency, and disintermediation of trusted third parties. The scalability trilemma: decentralization, security, and scalability are hard to maximize simultaneously — layer-2 solutions and new architectures address it. Institutional adoption, CBDCs (central bank digital currencies), and tokenization of real-world assets signal maturation. The King-level truth: the technology is genuinely transformative in specific domains, but ~90% of projects are speculation or scams — the skill is distinguishing the durable innovation from the noise, holding conviction through volatility, and never confusing price with value.

WORKED EXAMPLE: During a mania, thousands of tokens with no product reach billion-dollar valuations, then collapse to zero — while a handful of genuinely useful protocols survive multiple cycles and keep building. The King-level investor ignores the noise, evaluates real adoption and utility, and understands that transformative technology and rampant speculation coexist. Both are real; only one endures.
